To the hiring team at Kaikuvaara Oy,

A colleague at Suvanto mentioned your SAR antenna development over coffee last month, and I went home and read everything I could find about Kaikuvaara’s instrument programmes for airborne and spaceborne remote sensing. Building measurement hardware that has to work the first time in orbit, where nobody gets a second pass at a calibration sweep — that is the kind of engineering problem I have wanted to work on since I first studied antenna array theory as a graduate student. It is what made me want to write to you.

My MSc at Yangtze Delta Institute of Technology was in electrical engineering with a concentration in electromagnetics. The thesis was a simulation study of mutual coupling compensation in closely spaced patch antenna elements, which turned out to involve considerably more linear algebra and less physical intuition than I had expected going in. I chose YDIT for the antenna research group’s practical emphasis — we built and measured array prototypes, not only simulated them — and the coursework in microwave engineering, statistical signal processing, and numerical methods provided a foundation I still draw on daily. That grounding in both theory and physical hardware has shaped how I approach every design problem since.

What may not be obvious from the CV is the embedded side of my work at Boreal Photonics. Alongside maintaining the Python-based calibration pipeline, I wrote and debugged the C firmware for our real-time acquisition controller: an STM32F4 board handling ADC trigger sequencing and data packetisation over SPI. Getting the interrupt priorities and DMA transfer timing correct under hard real-time constraints was probably the most instructive six months of my career so far, and it left me much more comfortable working at the boundary between algorithm and hardware. I believe that boundary is exactly where Kaikuvaara’s instrument development lives, and it is where I want to be working.

I have also taken on team-lead responsibilities and am comfortable coordinating delivery across a small engineering group.

I would welcome a conversation about the Senior Signal Processing Engineer role. I have been based in Oulu since 2021, I am happy to stay, and I can make time at short notice.

Sami Korhonen

I took a parental leave from March 2020 to February 2021 and returned to a considerably more cautious buyer market. Honestly, it forced me to be sharper about qualifying opportunities and presenting value, which turned out to be the most useful professional development I never planned for.

My MSc from Kallavesi was in International Business, with a thesis on adoption barriers for industrial SaaS in Nordic markets. I won’t pretend that qualifies me as a signal processing engineer. But I know the Oulu industrial ecosystem at this point — I have sold into it for three years — and I believe companies at Kaikuvaara’s stage sometimes need someone who understands the commercial side of bringing technical instruments to market. If that is a conversation worth having, I am available and already local. If the role really is strictly engineering, I understand entirely and thank you for your time.

Freja Kovac

I spent three months living in Oulu last year for a field deployment, and by the end of it I was browsing rental listings. The city’s engineering community is smaller than Tampere’s or Helsinki’s but remarkably concentrated in RF and photonics — you run into the same people at Suvanto seminars and local industry events, which keeps collaboration straightforward and keeps everyone honest about the quality of their work. When I saw the Senior Signal Processing Engineer posting at Kaikuvaara, it felt like the right reason to make a permanent move.

That period was frustrating — I spent most of it requalifying through intensive short courses in FPGA design and real-time embedded systems, which in hindsight made me a considerably better engineer even though I would not recommend the circumstances. Since coming back in January 2021, my work has focused on digital beamforming for multi-channel sensor systems, including a satellite payload beamformer prototype that went through a full EORA subcontract review. That project was the most technically demanding I have worked on: sixteen elements, real-time calibration under hard power and latency constraints, and trade-offs at every design level.

The aspects of the Kaikuvaara role that stand out to me are the combination of algorithm development and close-to-hardware implementation. At Tuulikallio I spend roughly equal time writing beamforming algorithms in C for DSP processors and building the Python infrastructure to test and validate them, and I do my strongest work when I can move between those two levels rather than being confined to one. My MSc at the Sakura National University was in applied physics — wave propagation and array theory — and that analytical grounding still shapes how I approach new problems even when the application domain shifts. The constrained optimisation methods and statistical estimation framework I learned there are tools I reach for constantly.

I should also mention that I am comfortable with estimation-theoretic methods including Kalman filtering, which I understand may be relevant to some of Kaikuvaara’s tracking and calibration work.

What I can offer concretely: nine years building real-time spatial filtering systems, familiarity with the full path from simulation through embedded deployment, and a genuine desire to be in Oulu. I already know engineers in the local community from my time at the field trial, and I value the kind of place where people from different organisations actually talk to each other.

Available at your convenience.

Lukas Novak

application.cover_letter_markdown:
Building measurement instruments that need to function correctly on the first attempt — in orbit, where there is no second try — is what I want to be doing for the remaining years of my career. When I saw Kaikuvaara’s posting for a Senior Signal Processing Engineer, it was the first job listing in a long time that genuinely aligned with that ambition, and I felt it was worth reaching out.

I have spent most of my career at Polaris RF Labs here in Oulu, where I work on algorithm design and simulation for ground-based communications receiver systems. My core focus has been spectral estimation, interference mitigation, and adaptive filtering, working primarily in MATLAB and Simulink. The work is analytical rather than implementation-heavy: I design and verify algorithms at the system level, write the specifications, and hand them to the implementation team for deployment. Over the past several years my interest has shifted increasingly toward spatial processing, and I was responsible for the beamforming algorithm design on Polaris’s 8-element adaptive receiver prototype. That project involved computing real-time steering weights under co-channel interference and designing the calibration routine for gain and phase errors across the array elements. It was the first time I worked directly with a phased-array architecture rather than modelling one from a distance, and it changed the direction of what I want to do. Array signal processing, and specifically the kind of precision beamforming work that Kaikuvaara does for remote-sensing instruments, is where I want to put my effort going forward.

My degree is an MSc in Engineering Physics from Gotaalv University of Technology in Gothenburg, completed in 1999. The programme’s emphasis was on electromagnetic theory, mathematical physics, linear systems, and numerical methods — a curriculum oriented around principles rather than specific applications. That depth has paid off many times: when a design problem resists the textbook approach, I fall back on the physics-based framework I learned there and it rarely lets me down.

All of my professional work at Polaris has involved regular technical interaction with English-speaking partners and customers. For extended periods, including a multi-year collaboration with a UK-based systems integrator, the working language was entirely English. I am fully comfortable with technical writing, presentations, and daily communication in English.

I recognise that twenty-plus years at a single employer might read as a narrow profile. I see it differently: I stayed because the problems held my attention, and now I want to go where they are harder. I took a sabbatical in 2002–03 to travel and returned with a clearer sense of what I valued in work. The algorithmic experience I have built at Polaris transfers to Kaikuvaara’s instrument challenges more directly than the job titles might suggest.

I am in Oulu already, so relocation is not a factor. Happy to discuss at your convenience.

Antti Rantanen

To the hiring team at Kaikuvaara,

I will keep this straightforward. I have been working as a signal processing engineer at Tuulenkaari Satellite Systems since 2017, and I am looking for a role where the technical challenges are harder than what I currently have access to. The Senior Signal Processing Engineer position at Kaikuvaara looks like it could be that kind of step.

At Tuulenkaari my day-to-day work involves designing and validating signal processing algorithms for ground-segment telemetry processing — primarily filter chains, spectral estimation routines, and demodulation pipelines. It is solid engineering work but has become fairly repetitive over the years. I have reached the point where I know the problem space well enough that there is not much new to learn in it, and the projects coming through have not changed character meaningfully since I returned from leave in 2020. What I want is a role where the signal processing problems are harder and the consequences of getting them wrong are more immediate, which is what attracted me to Kaikuvaara’s work in remote-sensing instrumentation. The idea of working on systems where signal integrity directly determines whether a measurement campaign succeeds or fails is motivating in a way that routine ground-processing work is not any more.

My MSc from KUT was in electrical engineering, with a thesis on spectral distortion in multi-rate sampling systems. The theoretical foundations are solid, and I have built on them at Tuulenkaari with seven years of practical algorithm work in spectral analysis and demodulation for real downlink data. I think that combination of academic grounding and hands-on implementation is relevant to what Kaikuvaara does, even though the specific application domain differs. I also have familiarity with Kalman filtering and estimation theory, and have team-lead experience.

Some practical points: I am a Finnish citizen, so work authorisation is not an issue. I spent six weeks in Oulu in 2023 for a customer deployment and found the city genuinely appealing — I would relocate without hesitation if the role is right. All of my professional work at Tuulenkaari has been conducted in English alongside Finnish, because we collaborate regularly with EORA prime contractors and international partners.

I should be transparent: I had an extended medical leave from January 2019 to March 2020 that shows as a gap in my timeline. I have been back at full capacity since returning in April 2020, and it has not affected my work or reliability since.

I understand I may not cover every dimension of what you are looking for, and I am realistic about that. But the signal processing fundamentals are transferable, and I would welcome a conversation if you think there might be a fit.

Anne Heikkinen

I am a mechanical design engineer writing about your Senior Signal Processing Engineer opening, which I realise is not the most obvious match on paper. Let me explain why I think it is worth your time to read on.

I graduated from Politecnico del Naviglio in 2021 with a mechanical engineering degree and have spent the past five years at Raunio Engineering in Iisalmi, designing structural components for underground mining equipment. The FEA work, the simulation tuning, the cycle of predicting behaviour from first principles and then checking it against measured data: that is where I concentrate best and learn fastest.

That realisation led me to start studying signal processing and applied mathematics on my own, working through textbook problems and online courses in the evenings and on weekends. I have covered the basics of discrete-time systems, spectral analysis, and filter design. I will not pretend that self-study makes me qualified for a senior position in a field I have not practised professionally — that would be dishonest. But I believe the underlying analytical disciplines transfer more than job titles suggest. The comfort with numerical precision, the habit of verifying models against physical reality, the experience of designing systems where tolerances matter and failures have real consequences — these are things five years in heavy-machinery engineering have trained into me, and the systems we build are not forgiving of sloppiness.

I understand there is a real gap between my current profile and what you are looking for. If a junior role, a transitional position, or even a structured learning arrangement exists, I would welcome the conversation. If not, I appreciate you reading this far and wish you well finding the right person. I am reachable at the contact details on my CV.

Hannu Salo

application.cover_letter_markdown:
Kaikuvaara Oy — Senior Signal Processing Engineer

I have been following the growth of Oulu’s RF and photonics engineering community from a distance for several years, and Kaikuvaara’s work stands out within it. The phased-array antenna instruments you build for remote sensing sit close to what I have been doing at Meridian Defence Electronics for most of my career, and when I saw this posting I wanted to write before the listing closed.

My background is in array signal processing, which has been at the centre of my work since I joined Meridian in 2007. The core of what I do involves designing beamforming and spatial filtering algorithms for multi-element antenna systems in the electronic warfare domain — the kind of work where you spend weeks refining a simulation model and then discover on the bench that the real array has coupling characteristics the model entirely failed to capture. Nineteen years of that cycle has given me both the theoretical toolbox and a practical instinct for where simulations break down, and I think that combination of depth and scepticism is difficult to develop outside sustained hands-on algorithm work on fielded systems.

Some context on my qualifications. My MSc from Kallavesi — completed in 2006, when it was still Nuuksio Institute of Technology — was in electronics and electrical engineering with a specialisation in signal processing for communications systems. The programme was mathematically rigorous, and the thesis involved adaptive interference cancellation for wideband signals. The mathematical methods I learned there — constrained optimisation, the matrix algebra, the statistical estimation framework — are the foundation I still work from when designing spatial filters today. I have co-authored three papers in SESE conference proceedings on adaptive beamforming techniques, and I maintain a small open-source MATLAB toolbox for array signal processing simulation (github.example/example-lkhan/array-sim-toolbox) that gets used by a modest community of practitioners and students. On the practical side, I am a Finnish citizen and hold the right to work anywhere in the EU.

I have team-lead experience and am comfortable directing technical delivery across a small engineering group.

What attracts me to Kaikuvaara specifically, beyond the technical overlap, is the concentration of antenna and RF expertise in Oulu’s engineering community. The proximity of Suvanto’s antenna research group, the university’s radio engineering programme, and companies like yours creates an environment where ideas travel faster than they do here in the capital region. I have attended workshops and seminar days in Oulu over the years and consistently come away with something useful, which is not something I can say about most industry events.

I would welcome a conversation about the role and am happy to walk through any specific project in more detail.

Ling Khan
